Check each liquid for polarity first, bromine is a non-polar $\text{Br}_2$ molecule while the other three all contain polar bonds.

walkthrough:
**Recall what temporary dipole forces mean**

Think of these as London dispersion forces. They exist between all molecules.

The question asks which liquid has *only* these forces, so no permanent dipole-dipole forces and no hydrogen bonding.

**Test each substance for polarity and H-bonding**

Look at the structure of each particle in the liquid.

$\text{Br}_2$ is non-polar and symmetrical, with no H to H-bond. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are all polar, and ethanol and water can H-bond via O-H groups.

**Conclude the only London-only liquid**

Only non-polar bromine has induced dipole to induced dipole attractions alone.

The other three have London forces *plus* stronger permanent dipole or hydrogen bond interactions.

options.A: Bromine liquid consists of non-polar $\text{Br}_2$ molecules. With equal sharing of electrons and no permanent dipole, the only intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces from temporary dipoles.
options.B: Ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, has a polar O-H group. It shows London forces plus permanent dipole-dipole forces plus strong hydrogen bonding, so it is not London-only.
options.C: Hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, is a polar molecule with H bonded to electronegative Cl. It has London forces plus permanent dipole-dipole forces, so it is not London-only.
options.D: Water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, is polar and has two O-H bonds. It shows London forces plus dipole-dipole forces plus very strong hydrogen bonding, so it is not London-only.
